raw_comment:
1. I notice that more graduate students take online courses full-time when compared to other college levels, but most of the data for all college students was centered around a mix of both online and on-campus.  The data mimics that of a normal distribution which is surprising to me because I would think since COVID and the adaptations we had to do for online learning would sway the data that way.

2. I suppose there is no way to truly know, but I’m curious how many students would have chosen online learning if the pandemic hadn’t occurred.  Are they only choosing online learning because they became used to it or are there other underlying factors?

3. Many of our students still take courses at the physical campus because we only live an hour away from the more popular schools – Minot State & BSC.  There are still a few who take online courses so they can still work on their family’s ranch/farm.  As for adult learners, they take online courses because they need to work and/raise their family.  Personally speaking, I wouldn’t be able to work full-time and travel to the campus and I’m only taking one course.

4. “Is On-Campus Learning A Thing of the Past?”

raw_comment:
The stacked bar graph indicates four qualitative measures and it seems that sometime in near future there will be more online classes than in pre-pandemic time since the combination of on-campus and some online and a balance of campus/online as well as the majority- of online is much higher than on campus. This makes sense since the online logistics have been experimented during the pandemic and has responded with positive productivity and efficiency. 

For each educational program, there are differences: 
For example for traditional-aged undergraduates: most classes would be a combination of online and on-campus but the percentage of the majority online is the lowest among the three. 
For adult undergraduates, there are similarities with the graduates except that for graduates the proportion of majority online classes is higher than the adult undergraduates. 
Overall, it seems that the online classes'  logistics have proved to be efficient and productive based on the respondents of this survey.

raw_comment:
I notice that traditional-aged undergraduates are most likely to take classes on campus, little to no online or a balance of both than adult undergraduates and graduate students in 2025. Adult undergraduates and graduate students are less likely to take on campus classes and more likely to have a majority online classes or fully online, just less on campus classes. 

I wonder if the difference in percentages for the different groups of students has to do with what is easier for them to do, and if it improves their attendance to the classes. Also, I wonder if the pandemic/online classes are what could cause this change over the years for the students. Another thing I wonder is if it has to do with age and what they want to experience in college. 

This relates to my community and me because as a senior this year I have to choose whether to do online or on-campus classes. Also, the rest of the senior class has to decide and many have different opinions on it because of the past year where we had online and a bit of hybrid schedules. I think many of us would like to get the on campus experience, but some may not.

raw_comment:
I notice that for Graduate students the majority of them are online or are mostly online and partly on campus. Not accounting for covid and the shift to fully online school during lockdown, a lot of colleges were advertising online courses for adults that could not make it back to campus, they would be able to schedule their own courses. Now accounting for covids reach on education, we could see another spike in a variation of covid sending college students back or colleges giving students the option for health reasons. 

I wonder if rates on colleges change depending on whether it's in person or not. More so considering the amount of attention graduate students need regarding their work, from what I've heard from my teachers, some graduate level courses have as many as 15 students in a class. The amount of "intimacy" at those levels being lost could result in people potentially arguing that college admission should be less.

I'm graduating June of 2024 and I'd be going to college fall of 2024-spring of 2025, this would affect me because if this is a choice that I have to make it could alter my future and the futures of my peers. If I could take online courses it would be nice to be able to make my own schedule.

"A College Lecture on MY Couch, Nothing Better."

raw_comment:
What Do You Notice? 

I noticed that for traditional-aged undergraduates roughly 48% will be on campus most of the time. I noticed for adult undergraduates roughly 23% will be on campus most of the time. I noticed that graduate students roughly 5%  will be on campus most of the time. I notice that the younger crowd tends to be on campus more than the older crowds of college students. 

What Do You Wonder? 

I wonder how come the younger groups of people in college (undergraduates) may attend on campus. I wonder how were these predictions made. I wonder why more people decide to be online than on campus. 

How Does This Relate to You and Your Comunity? 

This relates to me and my community as I am going to be attending college in the fall of 2023 through the spring of 2027 meaning that I will be attending college through 2025. As a personal preference, I would be on campus full-time. 

Headline: 

Online Vs. On Campus: A Predicted Look at Colleges in 2025

raw_comment:
1.This graph illustrates how soon college courses might start to appear. There is an intriguing range of conceivable experiences in the future. The majority of undergraduates who are conventional age stand out since they receive the majority of their education on campus. Only 9% of this group's members are primarily online, while only 2% are completely online. The percentages for online instruction significantly increase for the adult undergraduate segment, reaching 32% for the majority and 9% for the entire course. With the greatest percentages of 34% majority and 17% totally online education, graduate students are anticipated to receive the least instruction in person. This demonstrates how graduate students are more inclined to enroll in online courses.
2.The major question I ponder is whether enrolling in online courses for graduate students is necessarily simpler. What would this graph have looked like before the pandemic drove schools to become virtual is another thing I ponder about. How education will change in the future and whether "conventional" college experiences will no longer be available. Did the pandemic cause any changes to this?
3.Because I'll be attending college the next year and am concerned that many of my classes will be online, this has an influence on me and my community. This influences how college students learn and how a person choose an institution.
4.The Future of College: Going Digital

raw_comment:
1.I noticed that for traditional aged undergrads, almost 50% will have classes majority on campus or fully. This is the complete opposite for grad students where over 50% will take classes majority or fully online. While adult undergrads are in between these 2 categories, adult undergrads have the most variety in the data. 
2.I wonder how this data would compare to 10 or 20 years ago when there were much less advancements in technology within education. I also wonder how this data may compare in 15 years as technology advances, will majority of traditional undergrads be fully online? And will the option for fully on campus education disappear? I wonder if graduation rates differ based on how college courses are taken? For example is there a higher graduation rate for grad students if their courses are taken fully online?

raw_comment:
1) According to the graph, most individuals choose a mix of in-person and online programs. By 2025, most traditional-aged undergraduate students will spend the bulk of their time at college learning on-campus, with 40% of that total number of students taking a mix of online and on-campus coursework. In comparison to the other two groups, graduate students have a much greater percentage of entirely online students. 

2) This makes me wonder if companies believe degrees obtained online are less legitimate or worthwhile. I'm also curious how much of this is related to the rising income disparity. Is it true that more people are going online since it is more affordable? I'm curious if the prediction made by 271 online officers is an accurate representation of all online officers at all institutions across the country. I wonder if the results of the graph were influenced by COVID-19. 

3) It is relevant to my community because how students experience college influences how many individuals are able to obtain a college education. More people in my town will be able to get a college degree as online learning becomes more widely available, providing my community with more people capable of doing tasks that need a college education. Perhaps a larger percentage of students will find themselves graduating because of the potential future of college.

4) The Future of College Education: Is Learning From Screens Inevitable?

raw_comment:
- What do you notice?
I noticed that most undergraduates are expected to experience college on campus more than graduate students. As for adult undergraduates, there is also a slight balance of on-campus and online with just a little more on the side of on-campus.

- What do you wonder?

- How does this relate to you and your community?

I too want to have a college experience on-campus to make up for the in person learning I have lost in high school and to stop feeling isolated and alone.

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I notice that both adult undergraduates and graduates had a minority of students fully on campus. On the other hand, traditional aged undergraduates' smallest amount was with those fully online, whereas the other two had a sizable chunk fully online. While traditional aged undergraduates lean heavily towards on campus classes with only some online, as you move to the others the numbers are more dispersed, being less heavily blue-leaning.
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder what these chief online officers are basing their expectations on, and how accurate they will come to be 
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because many of my classmates will soon be going to college, and as soon to be undergraduates, there's a definite allure to being in person and taking classes on campus.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
This graph depicts how chief online officers expect students nationwide to experience their classes. My title for this graph would be "Is Virtual or In-Person the Face of 2025 College Learning?"

What do you notice?

I notice that traditional-aged undergraduates have a big gap between adult undergraduates and graduate students for the Majority on campus, some online. I also notice that graduate students have the highest amount for being fully online by 17%.

What do you wonder? 

I wonder if age plays a major factor in whether or not it has more participation for being more or less on campus. I wonder about this, because traditional-aged undergraduates have the least amount for being fully online but the most balanced of campus/online. I wonder if that has to deal with the way they learn or their concentration depending on how they are learning.

How does this relate to you and your community?



This relates to me and my community, because this could show how it will mostly be like for my community to start going to college classes, and that the majority will have a well balance between online and campus, but as you start reaching graduate you lean to be more online than on campus.

What’s going on in this graph?

1. First of all, I notice that this graph is a prediction for the year 2025 and not accurate. Also, I notice that there is about a 50% decrease in majority on-campus, some online from traditional-aged undergraduates to adult undergraduates. Another thing is that they predict little change for balancing online and on-campus learning for traditional-aged, adult, and graduate students.

Another thing is if the people who are truly on campus are there because they want the "true college experience."

It also relates to me and my community because my senior class just got out of doing online learning/classes last year. Some people may have liked online learning to the point where they might want to try it again for college.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The biggest thing to notice in this graph is the lack of students and graduates entirely on campus with no online classes. When looking at the rest of the chart we see that there's a good amount of students with a balance of campus and online and a higher percentage of students that are online than the majority on campus. 

What do I wonder?
I wonder if these results are due to everyone getting accustomed to online classes during 2020. I wonder if the stats were like this before covid happened as well. I would like to see a side-by-side comparison from pre covid and after covid to determine if that is why more students stick to online. 

How does this relate to me and my community?
This relates to me and my community because I'm class of 2024 and will be applying for college sometime this year or next year. it is important for me to know how many college students are deciding to stay online and why? is it more convenient? and is it the choice I should make as well?

What's going on in this graph?
A catchy title for this graph could be 'Going to College or Going Remote? Majority of college students choosing to remain online."

3. This relates to me and my community because we had to experience having school online. To some people it was more difficult to adjust to it. But, this could have been a learning experience to see what kind of way they would like to go to college, online or on-campus. I also know someone who is a graduate student that has explained that having online classes if more beneficial for them because they have more time to do other things, which is similiar to what is seen in this graph for how classes could look like in 2025.

raw_comment:
I notice that almost no students will be fully on campus by 2025, and almost all students will be in an online class in one form or another. I also noticed the trend of graduate students being more gravitated toward online courses. 
I wonder why graduate and adult undergraduate students are more likely to take online classes, why the rates seem so similar between those two groups, and the traditional undergraduates lean so far toward on-campus learning. 
As more and more things become virtualized, I have to wonder just how much of our community will be part of institutions that are online. More and more things are being influenced by the leaps in online technology during the pandemic, from jobs to school to our hobbies. If high schools start going online, or a lot of jobs, it can change what I and many others have to expect when going into a job.
Online Strikes Back: Older students beginning to go virtual?

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that in this graph it's anticipated that most students would pursue their education online, as opposed to living entirely on campus and not online. This is fascinating because it is customary to study in person rather than electronically. Only 4% of conventional undergrad students are expected to have all of their classes on-campus by 2025. The number is even lower, at 2% or fewer, for graduate and adult undergraduate students taking all of their classes on campus. The bulk of classes are now being offered online, with a balance of on-campus instruction.

2) I wonder if COVID-19 has caused a movement toward online education. And if institutions will eventually eliminate the choice between taking classes on campus and online.

3) This affects me and my neighborhood since, like the rest of my classmates, I'll eventually attend college (the senior class). And while I'm not sure if we'll have that option during our first year, given that we'll be in college by the time 2025 rolls around, I assume we will.

4) Will we be stuck indoors or set free to roam?

raw_comment:
1.  I notice that as age increases the use predicted use of online classes also increases. For graduate students who are typically 33 years of age have a predicted 1% of students who would have fully online classes. They also have the highest amount of predicted students who are fully online at 17%. If we take a look at traditional-aged undergraduate students, they have a much higher percentage of students who have a majority in person classes. They also have the lowest amount of predicted students who are full online at 2%.

I also wonder if this graph was created using the information gathered from universities around the country during the pandemic.

3. The majority of the people around me are starting to enter college, where then we will need to decide if we want to learn remotely or in person. We are still in a post pandemic world, so it is important to keep in mind the benefits learning remotely provides.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that for traditional-aged undergraduates it is expected for them to experience their classes majority on campus, some online. On the other hand, adult undergraduates are expected to experience their classes with a balance of campus/online. 

What do you wonder?
	For adult undergraduates, the majority online/some on campus is 32. For graduate students, the majority online/some on campus is 34. This is significantly higher than for traditional-aged undergraduates. I wonder if this is a result of the responsibilities that come at different ages. Traditional-aged undergraduates attend college immediately after graduating high school. Adult undergraduates may have taken some time off after high school or they have other responsibilities so it is more beneficial for them to experience a balance between campus and online. While traditional-aged undergraduates might have more time on their hands and campus classes are what they want. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because I am a high school student and I graduate in 2024 so it is good to know what classes will look like for an undergraduate student. Some people may have thought that after the pandemic online classes would be over but they are still an option.  I think it is good that there is an online option for those who prefer that over on-campus classes.  

What’s going on in this graph?
The Normal in 2025: Online College

This graph predicts the manner of classes college students are likely to take in 2025.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the majority of the collected data prefer a hybrid schedule while a small amount wanted fully on-campus, with little, or no online. That's stating the obvious, but in a visual explanation, there's a skew seen in 4 out of the 5 categories for how students would like to do college. 

2. I understand why traditional-aged undergraduates would want classes in person because of the college experience. I wonder, though, are graduate students aiming for hybrid/online classes because they already experienced the typical "college life"? 

3. This relates to me in the sense that as a high school senior, when I applied for college, I aimed for classes that will take place in person as an undergraduate. I will soon fall under the traditional-aged undergraduate and be within the 4-44%. After the events of Covid-19 transitioning education to being taught online, several became used to it. With platforms like Zoom, it was obvious that their usage of them will grow even after the Covid-19 lockdown. By 2025, I'll be in my second year of college, so who knows what college would REALLY look like 2 years from now. All in the stats. 

HEADLINE:
Online, Hybrid, or In-Person? College Classes Take a Shift...

raw_comment:
1. This graph demonstrates the possible appearance of college classes in the near future.  There is an interesting array of future possible experiences.  The main thing that sticks out is how the traditional-aged undergraduates have the highest percentage for mostly on-campus instruction.  For this group, only 9% have the majority online with a mere 2% fully online.  With the adult undergraduate section, the online instruction percentages greatly increase to 32% for the majority and 9% for the full.  Graduate students have the lowest in-person projected instruction with the highest online percentages of 34% majority and 17% fully.  This showcases how it is more likely for graduate students to take online courses.
2. The main thing I wonder is if it is necessarily easier for graduate students to take online courses.  I also wonder what this graph would have looked like before the pandemic forced schools to go virtual.  Did the pandemic prove that online instruction is easier than one would think? How different schooling will be in the future, and if people will lose the “traditional” college experience. Did this all change because of the pandemic? 
3. This impacts me and my community because I will be attending college next year, and I worry that a lot of my classes will be virtual. This affects how those who attend college learn and how a person chooses a college. 
4. "Breaking Down the Future of American Colleges"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
From looking at this graph, I notice that online classes will continue to be a big part of education. For traditional aged undergraduate students, it is estimated that only 4% of them will experience a fully on campus experience. 
 
What do you wonder?
From looking at this graph, I wonder why online classes are still popular. From my own experience and from talking with my peers, online classes were not the best learning experience. Is it because more and more professors don’t want to come back?


What’s going on in this graph?
This graph depicts the data from an online survey, in which participants were asked how they felt college students will experience their classes. 


How does this relate to you and your community?
This graph relates to me because I will be in college in 2025 and am interested to know how many people believe I will be learning.

What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
I notice that the time frame was january-february 2022 by quality matters. The total number of responses were 271 from 4,700 college and university chief online officers. I've noticed that both completely online and completely in person are low percentages. The vast majority  of classes were the majority on campus and some online for traditional-aged undergraduates. Then a balance of online and on campus for both adult undergraduates and graduate students. I noticed that this was an estimation for what college classes look like in 2025.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because my school is fully in person. I'm unsure if we even offer an online option for when students get sick but this is reality. Majority of the world has to go through this which is the aftermath of the pandemic. Being the class of 2024 it affects me as I will be in college the same time class of 2025 is.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that this is not a graph of what is specifically happening now, but a prediction for the future. I notice that there are many different types of students listed. I also notice that a balance between online and on campus learning is mostly the majority. 
2. I wonder if these predictions are going to hold true or if something would drastically change how we learn again. (Like COVID-19 and how that impacted learning). 
3. This relates to me and my community because my community and myself have been impacted and affected by online learning. For a majority of my seventh and eighth grade years, I learned online. While I am not completely learning online anymore, it certainly has changed the way I do my schoolwork. 
4. Online Learning and Its Impact 5 Years Later

raw_comment: I find it interesting that strictly online learning is not more popular considering how convenient it is, especially for adult under grads. It can be accessible if you have good internet and if you have responsibilities like a job, family, etc. It is an easy way to still get your degree. That being said, I also wonder if certain skills sets will become more difficult to achieve. Being virtual can sometimes make it hard to retain information or build on leadership skills. As far as the impact online learning could have in the future, a lot of things could happen. It could allow for rural internet access, or it could lead to advances in technology. I'm also interested to see how the younger teens who had to endure virtual learning during the pandemic will respond to learning this way in college sense they already lived through it.

raw_comment:
What I notice in this graph is that it is especially rare for college students to be completely in-person or completely online. On all three levels of higher education, it is more common to have online and in-person time split up. Young undergraduates are more likely than the other groups to be completely online, but only by 2-3%. Graduate students, on the other hand, have a significantly higher rate of fully online students compared to the other two groups. 

I am curious why graduate students have such a significantly higher rate of online students. This also makes me curious whether employers think degrees achieved online are less credible or valuable. I also wonder how largely this relates to the growing wage gap. Are more people going online because it is more affordable?

This relates to me and my community because after experiencing the pandemic, I know college students who still experience online class even though they live on campus. I am also going to college soon and had to decide whether I wanted to participate in an online university.

A title for this graph is: "Online Alternatives Sweep the Nation"

raw_comment:
This graph shows a prediction for college classes in 2025. It shows that college is trending towards online courses. By 2025, for traditional-aged undergrad, only 4% are predicted to have fully on-campus classes. For adult undergrads and graduate students, the percentage is even less for fully on-campus classes, 2% or less. The trend for classes is going towards a balance of online and on-campus and the majority online. 

I wonder if the shift toward online classes is a result of COVID-19. This was not something that many colleges offered previous to COVID. I wonder if this will provide more access to schooling for people who may not be able to live on-campus or commute. I also wonder if this will affect things like tuition. 

This relates to my community as I am starting college in the fall of 2023. This means I will be graduating college in 2027. It seems that it is highly likely I will have some online classes. 

College Learning: Technological Takeover

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:    "Online or Remote: How Will College Classes Look in the Near Future?" by Alida of Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey; “College Evolved: The Transition from Campus to Online Learning” by Louis of Andover, Massachusetts; “Move-In to Log-In: The Changing Landscape of College Education” by Katie of Academy of  Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, New Jersey; “Face-to-Face vs. Networked  Learning.  What's Coming for Different College Students?” by KC2025 from San Francisco and “Learning in the Information Age: How Will College Evolve in the Coming Years?” by Sandra from Massachusetts.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Jan. 20 to see the Reveal with the free link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.
 
Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is thrilled to be teaching some of her students in-person, and Ellen Thompson of Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada, who didn't mind teaching remotely in her pajamas.

raw_comment:
I notice that the graph is inconsistent based on the level of learning. The majority of college classes for traditional-aged undergraduates are on campus, with some online, and the least amount of classes being fully online. I also noticed that the group with the most online classes is the graduate students. This may be because many graduate students take their courses online instead of having to go to campus for class. The adult undergraduates and graduate students seem to have more classes online than the traditional-aged undergraduates do.  I wonder if students prefer online classes or on-campus classes?  This relates to me because I have experienced much of my recent years of school online and inconsistently in person. Online school can be difficult for many people to benefit from and it does not give the same college experience.

raw_comment: I notice that the age of the graph affects the type of learning. Traditional-aged undergrads are expected to have most on-campus classes with some optional online. It might be easier for them to take classes in the evening or around their working schedule. I wonder why some students prefer online learning over in-person learning. raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that most traditionally-aged undergraduates prefer to be mostly on campus while both adult undergraduates and graduates either prefer a balance of campus and online instruction or a majority of it to be online instruction. I also noticed that there is no percentage for graduate students that want to be fully on campus while it’s at 4% and 2% for traditionally aged and adult undergraduates respectively. It also seems that the graduate students have the most symmetrical distribution compared to the other two.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if graduate students prefer online instruction over in-person instruction as a result of being older and having to deal with more responsibilities, or if it’s due to something else. I also wonder what the 271 chief online officers based their answers on and why they believe that more graduate students would prefer online instruction than traditionally aged undergraduates 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because there are many seniors who plan on going to college and some of them may prefer to be instructed fully online while others may want a traditional college experience and be instructed in-person on campus.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that there is a small percentage of graduate students that are fully on-campus, there is not even a number on the graph to represent this group of people. In contrast, traditional-aged undergraduates are hardly online, with only 2% of them being fully online. Adult graduates can be seen to be similar to traditional-aged graduates since they are more on-campus in comparison to being fully online.

2. I wonder if, in the future, colleges will transition to fully online due to the percentages of graduate students. I wonder if COVID played a role in these percentages, when students had remote learning during high school and if it had them adapt to online learning compared to attending school physically.

3. This relates to my community because my classmates have gone through remote learning and I have seen students in my community prefer remote learning to physically attending school.

4. Apply Now to Digital College! Will On-Campus Cease to Exist in the Future?

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
According to these officers, a very small percentage of students, regardless of level, will be fully on-campus. The highest percentage for fully on-campus was 4% for traditional-aged undergraduates, a very small number. 
There also appears to be a statistically significant difference between the projected percentages for the different types of students, suggesting that there is an association between the type of student (traditional-aged undergraduates, adult undergraduates, and graduate students) and how the student is expected to experience college. 
Furthermore, it appears that traditional-aged undergraduates are the more likely to experiences college on-campus, as the percentage of this group projected to be fully on-campus, majority on-campus, and a balance of campus/online are all greater than those percentages for the other groups, while the percentages for majority online, some on-campus and fully online are both the lowest out of all the groups. Potentially, this could be because traditional-aged undergraduates do not, generally, have full-time jobs and other outside commitments that would prevent them from attending school physically. 
I also notice that this study is limited by nonresponse bias, as only 271 responses were received from a total attempted sample of 4,700, and these people, who were willing to respond, likely have stronger or differing opinions from those who did not respond.

raw_comment:
I noticed that by 2025, most traditional-aged undergraduate students will spend the majority of their time at college learning on-campus, with 40% of that total number of students having a balance of classes online and on campus. About 21% of adult undergraduates have classes on-campus, while 36% have a balance of campus and online learning. Then, 15% of graduate students have on-campus classes, and most have classes online. This makes me wonder how different schooling will be in the future, and if people will lose the “traditional” college experience.  Did this all change because of the pandemic? How will such a dependence on technology be both beneficial and detrimental in the future? This impacts me and my community because I will be attending college next year, and I worry that a lot of my classes will be virtual. 
Headline: The Future of Online and On-Campus Learning

raw_comment:
I noticed that more people like the hybrid version of being on campus and online, whether it was the majority on campus and some online or vice versa. 

I wonder if this trend of being on campus and online will continue to be an option in an increasingly technical world. About 44% of traditional-aged undergraduates students favor the majority on-campus, and some online option. About 40% of traditional undergraduates favor a balance of on-campus and online option. About 36% of adult undergraduates favor the balance of on-campus and online option. And 33% of graduate students favor on-campus and online option. 

There's an association between the grade level and the types of classes they'll take because the percentage of statistics doesn't match up with the segmented bar graph.

The data relates to my community because most senior high school students are in the process of applying to and waiting for acceptance to colleges. And this data matters because everyone has different preferences and priorities, which means their college schedule has to work around their time and choices, despite the college’s requirements to graduate.

More undergraduates and graduate students tend to favor attending the campus in-person and online.

raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the possible appearance of college classes in the near future.  There is an interesting array of future possible experiences.  The main thing that sticks out is how the traditional-aged undergraduates have the highest percentage for mostly on-campus instruction.  For this group, only 9% have majority online with a mere 2% fully online.  With the adult undergraduate section the online instruction percentages greatly increase to 32% for majority and 9% for fully.  Graduate students have the lowest in-person projected instruction with the highest online percentages of 34% majority and 17% fully.  This showcases how it is more likely for graduate students to take online courses.  The main thing I wonder is if it is necessarily easier for graduate students to take online courses.  I also wonder what this graph would have looked like before the pandemic forced schools to go virtual.  Did the pandemic prove that online instruction is easier than one would think?  This affects my community and I because almost all students across the nation have experienced online classes so it is necessary to understand whether or not that will be the case in college.  I would entitle this graph: "Future of College Classes."

raw_comment:
I noticed that there is little belief that students will experience college fully on campus with little to no online classes, with no more than 4 percent of officers expecting fully on-campus courses in any of the grade levels. We can also see that there is an association between education level and the prediction for their class types. Further, I notice that this data cannot be used to determine class types only predict those class types. We know this because this is an observational study in the form of a survey rather than an experiment. 

I wonder if predictions are based on calculations or are predicted based on qualitative observations. I also wonder if the expected information has been skewed or biased due to the events of COVID-19. 

This relates to me and my community as many students in my community are heading into college soon and I will be going into my first year of college in 2024-2025. 

This graph could be titled "Hybrid in Higher Education? Breaking Down the Future of American Colleges".

raw_comment:
What Do I Notice?
I notice that most people currently enrolled in college are doing more time on campus than those who have already graduated and it seems that younger students prioritize on-campus learning.

What do I wonder?
I wonder about the reasons why younger students would rather be on campus. Is it for the experience, or do they truly think it will benefit them more to be in person? I also wonder why graduates chose online more often.

How does this relate to me? 
This relates to me because my peers and I are currently at a period in our lives in which we are thinking about our futures and what colleges to go to, or whether or not we even want to go to one.

What's going on in this graph?
In this graph, we are seeing the difference in the types of learning that current students or past students prioritized.

raw_comment:
Based on the graph, as students get older & decide to get a high education, there is a more likely chance that they learn or pass their chosen degree online. It could be shown as you compare the fully online section, for traditional-aged undergrads (freshly out of high school), they only have 2 that participate fully online, for adult grads they have 9, then for graduate students have 17. It gradually increases as they get older.  The factors that may cause this is having a family, they may not being able to balance going on campus more often due to having to take care of them (regardless of age), along with other responsibilities (jobs & bills). 

This relates to me & my community because we are entering the age where we have to look for desirable colleges & picking what we may want to pursue as a career. Depending on what we want to do, there may be only certain things that may follow with that particular degree, the availability of it being either online, on campus or a mixture of both. That may make an impact on what people may strive for & how they may learn overall. I have seen firsthand how that may impact how well someone may do. As someone myself dealing with online & on campus. 

A good title for this graph may be "The Evolution of Online Vs. On-Campus Learning".

raw_comment:
What do I notice? 
- The largest number of prospective students who would go majority on-campus are traditional-aged undergraduates. 
- The group which has the largest number of those who would go fully online is graduate students. 
- The graduate student group has the most diversity regarding choices. 
What do I wonder? 
- Why are the numbers of students who want to be on-campus fully so low? 
- Why is the generally most common choices a balance between on-campus and online? 
- Did COVID-19 and quarantine have an impact on the possible higher rate of online college? 
What do I think is going on in this graph? 
- I think this graph is showing the expectation of how students in 2025 will attend college. The three groups are traditional-aged undergraduates, adult undergraduates, and graduate students. The options they can choose are fully on-campus, majority on-campus, balance between online and campus, majority online, and fully online. 
How does this relate to you and your community? 
- This relates to me and my community because I know many people of different age groups who are attending college. From what I have seen, the people who are traditional-aged undergraduates have gravitated towards a balance of on-campus and online. People in college who are older who I have seen have definitely chosen online school over on-campus.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph displays a prediction by college online officers of how they think their students will be learning – in-person, online or a hybrid, in 2025.  Note the source of the data.  Also, “traditional-aged undergraduates” are students less than 25-years old. 

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these graphs.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

There will be no “What’s Going On In This Graph?” next week.  The next graph will be released by Friday, January 27 with moderation on Wednesday, February 1.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that it is predicted that traditional-aged undergraduates and adult undergraduates have a balance between on-campus and online. For graduate students, it is predicted that the majority will be online and some will be on campus. For all three categories, less than 20% are predicted to stay fully online. In addition, all three categories are less than 10% likely to stay fully on-campus with little or no online learning. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why it is predicted that graduate students are mainly online and only some are on campus. I also wonder if this prediction will be accurate in the future.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because I will be in college in 2025. This relates to my community because some of my colleagues might be online while I am in person. 

Title: Online vs. In-person; College Edition

raw_comment:
1) I've noticed that traditional-aged undergraduates spend most of their time on campus and only a tiny percentage of their time online. Graduate students appear to have a more balanced schedule by shifting from online to on-campus, despite spending more time online than their counterparts.

2) I'm curious if the fact that adult undergraduates and graduate students spend more time online and appear to have a more balanced schedule than traditional-aged undergraduates is due to the responsibilities they have as working adults with families and other extreme commitments outside of school. It's easy to see how being online could make this lifestyle more bearable.

3) This is relevant to my community because the vast majority of seniors in my school who are attending college are doing so at a traditional age and prefer to live on campus and experience their classes that way. But when you talk to teachers who are trying to obtain their master's degrees they are most likely always online because they don't have the time or resources to attend campus all the time.

4) THE FUTURE OF COLLEGE LEARNING

raw_comment:
1.For tradition-aged undergraduates, the highest percentage lied in the section of Majority on-campus some online. For adult undergraduates, A balance of campus/online was the most frequent educational style. For graduate students, Majority online some on-campus classes were the most used. A pattern is seen where undergraduates prefer in person classes but then as they further their education, transition to online classes. To further this claim, only 2-9% of undergraduates are fully online whereas 17% of graduates are fully online. I also noticed is that not a lot of students are fully on campus: only 1-4% of undergraduates and graduates are fully online. 
2. What advantages can students find in choosing online courses over traditional ones? Do particular majors and courses encourage online work among their students?
3. This relates to me and my community as I have experienced online courses for two years for my first two years of high school as well as one month of online courses my junior year due to a surge of cases of the virus. I feel that online courses had a toll on my mental health as I was stuck in the same room for months on end. I also felt burdened with large amounts of work that my teachers expected to be done by the end of the day. I barely found any time for myself because I was so absorbed in my assignments.

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I notice that traditional undergraduate students prefer physical classrooms with little to no online course while nontraditional students tend to prefer online courses only. However, it is noticed that more commonly, students prefer to have a balance of both on-campus and online learning.

2) What do you wonder?
I wonder why graduate students majorly prefer online learning over in person learning. I also wonder what this graph would look like if it were given to professors/instructors because there are always mixed emotions on the topic of remote learning.  

3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I as we all had to attend school both physically and virtually. Many students have formed opinions on virtual learning and whether they prefer it over physical learning. If our school gave us the option to choose just as colleges are doing, our graphs would also fluctuate as there are many students who prefer one way of learning over the other. This graph also pertains to me since I will be entering college next year  and I may be presented with the decision of learning remotely or in person.

4) What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
"Online or Remote: How will college classes look in the near future?"
